entries.a1e4cfc3c692162d478e2e9af925f2e330b722a3: <div sID="gen15860" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Isa.18" sID="Isa.18"/> <div eID="gen15860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15861" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15862" type="x-p"/> Whatever country it is that is meant here by "the land shadowing with wings," here is a woe denounced against it, for God has, upon his people's account, a quarrel with it. I. They threaten God's people, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. All the neighbours are hereupon called to take notice what will be the issue, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. Though God seem unconcerned in the distress of his people for a time, he will at length appear against their enemies and will remarkably cut them off, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4-Isa.18.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. IV. This shall redound very much to the glory of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">ver. 7</reference>.
entries.5f860f50ca9f760c92779cfc04bb3362758dd9c6: <div eID="gen15862" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15861" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Denounced. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15863" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to the land shadowing with wings, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> beyond the rivers of Ethiopia: <hi type="super">2</hi> That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation scattered and peeled, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden down, whose land the rivers have spoiled! <hi type="super">3</hi> All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye. <hi type="super">4</hi> For so the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, I will take my rest, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, <hi type="italic">and</hi> like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. <hi type="super">5</hi> For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away <hi type="italic">and</hi> cut down the branches. <hi type="super">6</hi> They shall be left together unto the fowls of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth: and the fowls shall summer upon them, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon them. <hi type="super">7</hi> In that time shall the present be brought unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts of a people scattered and peeled, and from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation meted out and trodden under foot, whose land the rivers have spoiled, to the place of the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the mount Zion. <div eID="gen15863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15864" type="x-p"/> Interpreters are very much at a loss where to find this land that lies beyond the rivers of Cush. Some take it to be Egypt, a maritime country, and full of rivers, and which courted Israel to depend upon them, but proved broken reeds; but against this it is strongly objected that the next chapter is distinguished from this by the title of <hi type="italic">the burden of Egypt.</hi> Others take it to be Ethiopia, and read it, <hi type="italic">which lies near,</hi> or <hi type="italic">about, the rivers of Ethiopia,</hi> not that in Africa, which lay south of Egypt, but that which we call <hi type="italic">Arabia,</hi> which lay east of Canaan, which Tirhakah was now king of. He thought to protect the Jews, as it were, under <hi type="italic">the shadow of his wings,</hi> by giving a powerful diversion to the king of Assyria, when he made a descent upon his country, at the time that he was attacking Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.9">2 Kings xix. 9</reference>. But though by his ambassadors he bade defiance to the king of Assyria, and encouraged the Jews to depend upon him, God by the prophet slights him, and will not go forth with him; he may take his own course, but God will take another course to protect Jerusalem, while he suffers the attempt of Tirhakah to miscarry and his Arabian army to be ruined; for the Assyrian army shall become a present or sacrifice to the Lord of hosts, and to the place of his name, by the hand of an angel, not by the hand of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">v. 7</reference>. This is a very probable exposition of this chapter. But from a hint of Dr. Lightfoot's, in his Harmony of the Old Testament, I incline to understand this chapter as a prophecy against Assyria, and so a continuation of the prophecy in the <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">last three verses</reference> of the foregoing chapter, with which therefore this should be joined. That was against the army of the Assyrians which rushed in upon Judah; this is against the land of Assyria itself, which lay beyond the rivers of Arabia, that is, the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, which bordered on <hi type="italic">Arabia Deserta.</hi> And in calling it <hi type="italic">the land shadowing with wings</hi> he seems to refer to what he himself had said of it (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">ch. viii. 8</reference>), that <hi type="italic">the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel!</hi> The prophet might perhaps describe the Assyrians by such dark expressions, not naming them, for the same reason that St. Paul, in his prophecy, speaks of the Roman empire by a periphrasis: <hi type="italic">He who now letteth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7">2 Thess. ii. 7</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen15864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15865" type="x-p"/> I. The attempt made by this land (whatever it is) upon <hi type="italic">a nation scattered and peeled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">v. 2</reference>. Swift messengers are sent by water to proclaim war against them, as a nation marked by Providence, and <hi type="italic">meted out,</hi> to be trodden under foot. Whether this refer to the Ethiopians waging war with the Assyrians, or the Assyrians with Judah, it teaches us, 1. That a people which have been terrible from their beginning, have made a figure and borne a mighty sway, may yet become scattered and peeled, and may be spoiled even by their own rivers, that should enrich both the husbandman and the merchant. Nations which have been formidable, and have kept all in awe about them, may by a concurrence of accidents become despicable and an easy prey to their insulting neighbours. 2. Princes and states that are ambitious of enlarging their territories will always have some pretence or other to quarrel with those whose countries they have a mind to. "It is a nation that has been terrible, and therefore we must be revenged on it; it is now a nation scattered and peeled, meted out and trodden down, and therefore it will be an easy prey for us." Perhaps it was not brought so low as they represented it. God's people are trampled on as a nation scattered and peeled; but whoever think to swallow them up may find them still as terrible as they have been from their beginning; they are cast down, but not deserted, not destroyed. <div eID="gen15865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15866" type="x-p"/> II. The alarm sounded to the nations about, by which they are summoned to take notice of what God is about to do, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">v. 3</reference>. The Ethiopians and Assyrians have their counsels and designs, which they have laid deep, and promise themselves much from, and, in prosecution of them, send their ambassadors and messengers from place to place; but let us now enquire what the great God says to all this. 1. <hi type="italic">He lifts up an ensign upon the mountains, and blows a trumpet,</hi> by which he proclaims war against the enemies of his church, and calls in all her friends and well-wishers into her service, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">v. 3</reference>. He gives notice that he is about to do some great work, as <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts.</hi> 2. All the world is bidden to take notice of it; all the dwellers on earth must see the ensign and hear the trumpet, must observe the motions of the divine providence and attend the directions of the divine will. Let all enlist under God's banner, and be on his side, and hearken to the trumpet of his word, which gives not an uncertain sound. <div eID="gen15866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15867" type="x-p"/> III. The assurance God gives to his prophet, by him to be given to his people, that, though he might seem for a time to sit by as an unconcerned spectator, yet he would certainly and seasonably appear for the comfort of his people and the confusion of his and their enemies (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">So the Lord said unto me.</hi> Men will have their saying, but God also will have his; and, as we may be sure his word shall stand, so he often whispers it in the ears of his servants the prophets. When he says, <hi type="italic">I will take my rest,</hi> it is not as if he were weary of governing the world, of as if he either needed or desired to retire from it and repose himself; but it intimates that the great God has a perfect, undisturbed, enjoyment of himself, in the midst of all the agitations and changes of this world (the Lord sits even upon the floods unshaken; the Eternal Mind is always easy), and, though he may sometimes seem to his people as if he took not wonted notice of what is done in this lower world (they are tempted to think he is <hi type="italic">as one asleep,</hi> or <hi type="italic">as one astonished,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Ps. xliv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jer. xiv. 9</reference>), yet even then he knows very well what men are doing and what he himself will do. <div eID="gen15867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15868" type="x-p"/> 1. He will take care of his people, and be a shelter to them. He will regard his <hi type="italic">dwelling-place;</hi> his eye and his heart are, and shall be, upon it for good continually. Zion is his rest for ever, where he will dwell; and he will <hi type="italic">look after it</hi> (so some read it); he will lift up the light of his countenance upon it, will consider over it what is to be done, and will be sure to do all for the best. He will adapt the comforts and refreshments he provides for his people to the exigencies of their case; and they will <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> be acceptable, because seasonable. (1.) Like a clear heat after rain (so the margin), which is very reviving and pleasant, and makes the herbs to flourish. (2.) Like a dew and <hi type="italic">a cloud in the heat of harvest,</hi> which are very welcome, the dew to the ground and the cloud to the labourers. Note, There is that in God which is a shelter and refreshment to his people in all weathers and arms them against the inconveniences of every change. Is the weather cool? There is that in his favour which will warm them. Is it hot? There is that in his favour which will cool them. Great men have their winter-house and their summer-house (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">Amos iii. 15</reference>); but those that are at home with God have both in him. <div eID="gen15868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15869" type="x-p"/> 2. He will reckon with his and their enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.5-Isa.18.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. When the Assyrian army promises itself a plentiful harvest in the taking of Jerusalem and the plundering of that rich city, when the bud of that project is perfect, before the harvest is gathered in, while the sour grape of their enmity to Hezekiah and his people is ripening in the flower and the design is just ready to be put in execution, God shall destroy that army as easily as the husbandman cuts off the sprigs of the vine with pruning hooks, or because the grape is sour and good for nothing, and will not be cured, <hi type="italic">takes away and cuts down the branches.</hi> This seems to point at the overthrow of the Assyrian army by a destroying angel, when the dead bodies of the soldiers were scattered like the branches and sprigs of a wild vine, which the husbandman has cut to pieces. <hi type="italic">And they shall be left to the fowls of the mountains, and the beasts of the earth,</hi> to prey upon, both winter and summer; for as God's people are protected all seasons of the year, both in cold and heat (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">v. 4</reference>), so their enemies are at all seasons exposed; birds and beasts of prey shall both summer and winter upon them, till they are quite ruined. <div eID="gen15869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15870" type="x-p"/> IV. The tribute of praise which should be brought to God from all this (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that time,</hi> when this shall be accomplished, <hi type="italic">shall the present be brought unto the Lord of hosts.</hi> 1. Some understand this of the conversion of the Ethiopians to the faith of Christ in the latter days, of which we have the specimen and beginning in Philip's baptizing the Ethiopian eunuch, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.27">Acts viii. 27</reference>, &c. Those that were <hi type="italic">a people scattered and peeled, meted out, and trodden down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">v. 2</reference>), shall be a present to the Lord: and, though they seem useless and worthless, they shall be an acceptable present to him who judges of men by the sincerity of their faith and love, not by the pomp and prosperity of their outward condition. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> the gospel was ministered to the Gentiles that <hi type="italic">the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Rom. xv. 16</reference>. It is prophesied (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">Ps. lxviii. 31</reference>) that <hi type="italic">Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God.</hi> 2. Others understand it of the spoil of Sennacherib's army, out of which, as usual, presents were brought to <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.31.50">Num. xxxi. 50</reference>. It was the present of a people scattered and peeled. (1.) It was won from the Assyrians, who were now themselves reduced to such a condition as they scornfully described Judah to be in, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">v. 1</reference>. Those that unjustly trample upon others shall themselves be justly trampled upon. (2.) It was offered by the people of God, who were, in disdain, called <hi type="italic">a people scattered and peeled.</hi> God will put honour upon his people, though men put contempt upon them. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Observe, The present that is brought to the Lord of hosts must be brought <hi type="italic">to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts;</hi> what is offered to God must be offered in the way that he has appointed; we must be sure to attend him, and expect him to meet us, where he records his name.  <chapter eID="Isa.18"/> <div eID="gen15870" type="x-p"/>

entries.b5e138bcd28f8d42aa44bddea0ebf794bb2dd57e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8638"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <div sID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Is 18:1-7</reference>.<div eID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> Isaiah announces the overthrow of Sennacherib's hosts and desires the Ethiopian ambassadors, now in Jerusalem, to bring word of it to their own nation; and he calls on the whole world to witness the event (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">Is 18:3</reference>). As <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">Is 17:12-14</reference> announced the presence of the foe, so <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Is 18:1-7</reference> foretells his overthrow.<div eID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8638"/><hi type="bold">1. Woe--</hi>The heading in English Version, "God will destroy the Ethiopians," is a mistake arising from the wrong rendering "Woe," whereas the Hebrew does not express a threat, but is an appeal calling attention (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.6">Zec 2:6</reference>): "Ho." He is not speaking against but to the Ethiopians, calling on them to hear his prophetical announcement as to the destruction of their enemies.<div eID="gen14209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadowing with wings--</hi>rather, "land of the winged bark"; that is, "barks with wing-like sails, answering to vessels of bulrushes" in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Is 18:2</reference>; the word "rivers," in the parallelism, also favors it; so the Septuagint and Chaldee [Ewald]. "Land of the clanging sound of wings," that is, armies, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>; the rendering "bark," or "ship," is rather dubious [Maurer]. The armies referred to are those of Tirhakah, advancing to meet the Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.9">Is 37:9</reference>). In English Version, "shadowing" means protecting--stretching out its wings to defend a feeble people, namely, the Hebrews [Vitringa]. The Hebrew for "wings" is the same as for the idol Cneph, which was represented in temple sculptures with wings (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Psa 91:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beyond--</hi>Meroe, the island between the "rivers" Nile and Astaboras is meant, famed for its commerce, and perhaps the seat of the Ethiopian government, hence addressed here as representing the whole empire: remains of temples are still found, and the name of "Tirhakah" in the inscriptions. This island region was probably the chief part of Queen Candace's kingdom (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.27">Ac 8:27</reference>). For "beyond" others translate less literally "which borderest on."<div eID="gen14211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ethiopia--</hi>literally, "Cush." Horsley is probably right that the ultimate and fullest reference of the prophecy is to the restoration of the Jews in the Holy Land through the instrumentality of some distant people skilled in navigation (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Is 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">Is 60:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">Psa 45:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">68:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.10">Zep 3:10</reference>). Phoenician voyagers coasting along would speak of all Western remote lands as "beyond" the Nile's mouths. "Cush," too, has a wide sense, being applied not only to Ethiopia, but Arabia-Deserta and Felix, and along the Persian Gulf, as far as the Tigris (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.13">Ge 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen14212" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c2c6cb163322183022cf4b743cfabc8dcc4ba1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8639"/><div sID="gen14213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8639"/><hi type="bold">2. ambassadors--</hi>messengers sent to Jerusalem at the time that negotiations passed between Tirhakah and Hezekiah against the expected attack of Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.9">Is 37:9</reference>).<div eID="gen14213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by ... sea--</hi>on the Nile (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">Is 19:5</reference>): as what follows proves.<div eID="gen14214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vessels of bulrushes--</hi>light canoes, formed of papyrus, daubed over with pitch: so the "ark" in which Moses was exposed (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.3">Ex 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Go--</hi>Isaiah tells them to take back the tidings of what God is about to do (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Is 18:4</reference>) against the common enemy of both Judah and Ethiopia.<div eID="gen14216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scattered and peeled--</hi>rather, "strong and energetic" [Maurer]. The Hebrew for "strong" is literally, "drawn out" (Margin; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.10">Psa 36:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Ec 2:3</reference>). "Energetic," literally, "sharp" (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Ha 1:8</reference>, Margin; the verb means to "sharpen" a sword, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.15">Eze 21:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.16">16</reference>); also "polished." As Herodotus (3:20, 114) characterizes the Ethiopians as "the tallest and fairest of men," G. V. Smith translates, "tall and comely"; literally, "extended" (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Is 45:14</reference>, "men of stature") and polished (the Ethiopians had "smooth, glossy skins"). In English Version the reference is to the Jews, scattered outcasts, and loaded with indignity (literally, "having their hair torn off," Horsley).<div eID="gen14217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terrible--</hi>the Ethiopians famed for warlike prowess [Rosenmuller]. The Jews who, because of God's plague, made others to fear the like (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">De 28:37</reference>). Rather, "awfully remarkable" [Horsley]. God puts the "terror" of His people into the surrounding nations at the first (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.27">Ex 23:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.2.9">Jos 2:9</reference>); so it shall be again in the latter days (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.2">Zec 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen14218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from ... beginning hitherto--</hi>so English Version rightly. But Gesenius, "to the terrible nation (of upper Egypt) and further beyond" (to the Ethiopians, properly so called).<div eID="gen14219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meted out--</hi>Hebrew, "of line." The measuring-line was used in destroying buildings (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Is 34:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">2Ki 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">La 2:8</reference>). Hence, actively, it means here "a people meting out,--an all-destroying people"; which suits the context better than "meted," passively [Maurer]. Horsley, understanding it of the Jews, translates it, "Expecting, expecting (in a continual attitude of expectation of Messiah) and trampled under foot"; a graphic picture of them. Most translate, of strength, strength (from a root, to brace the sinews), that is, a most powerful people.<div eID="gen14220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trodden down--</hi>true of the Jews. But Maurer translates it actively, a people "treading under foot" all its enemies, that is, victorious (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Is 14:25</reference>), namely, the Ethiopians.<div eID="gen14221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spoiled--</hi>"cut up." The Nile is formed by the junction of many streams in Abyssinia, the Atbara, the Astapus or Blue river (between which two rivers Meroe, the "Ethiopia" here meant, lies), and the Astaboras or White river; these streams wash down the soil along their banks in the "land" of Upper Egypt and deposit it on that of Lower Egypt. G. V. Smith translates it, "Divide." Horsley takes it figuratively of the conquering armies which have often "spoiled" Judea. <div eID="gen14222" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e32167bbf9e23f521267a697654c854d111e564: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8640"/><div sID="gen14223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8640"/><hi type="bold">3. see ye ... hear ye--</hi>rather, "ye shall see ... shall hear." Call to the whole earth to be witnesses of what Jehovah ("He") is about to do. He will "lift up an ensign," calling the Assyrian motley hosts together (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>) on "the mountains" round Jerusalem, to their own destruction. This (the eighteenth chapter) declares the coming overthrow of those armies whose presence is announced in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">Is 17:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">13</reference>. The same motive, which led Hezekiah to seek aid from Egypt, led him to accept gladly the Ethiopian Tirhakah's aid (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Is 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.9">37:9</reference>). Ethiopia, Egypt, and Judea were probably leagued together against the common enemy, 713 B.C. See notes on the twenty-second chapter, where a difference of tone (as referring to a different period) as to Ethiopia is observable. Horsley takes the "ensign" to be the cross, and the "trumpet" the Gospel trumpet, which shall be sounded more loudly in the last days. <div eID="gen14223" type="x-p"/>
entries.722e0571c3bce955fc817df36f99c27581c60dd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8641"/><div sID="gen14224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8641"/><hi type="bold">4. take ... rest ... consider--</hi>I will calmly look on and not interpose, while all seems to promise success to the enemy; when figuratively, "the sun's heat" and "the night dews" ripen their "harvest"; but "before" it reaches its maturity I will destroy it (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.5">Is 18:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen14224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like a clear heat--</hi>rather, "at the time of the clear (serene) heat" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon herbs--</hi>answering to "harvest" in the parallel clause. Maurer translates, "in the sunlight" (<reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.21">37:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.4">Ha 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like ... dew--</hi>rather, "at the time of the dew cloud." God's "silence" is mistaken by the ungodly for consent; His delay in taking vengeance for forgetfulness (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.21">Psa 50:21</reference>); so it shall be before the vengeance which in the last day shall usher in the restoration of the Jews (Is 34:1-8; 57:11, end of the verse, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3-2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:3-10</reference>). <div eID="gen14227" type="x-p"/>
entries.a062b0e5262ea042e74c6a7a71f5495c1c77bfa6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8642"/><div sID="gen14228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8642"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>rather, "But."<div eID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect--</hi>perfected. When the enemy's plans are on the verge of completion.<div eID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sour grape ... flower--</hi>rather, "when the flower shall become the ripening grape" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sprigs--</hi>the shoots with the grapes on them. God will not only disconcert their present plans, but prevent them forming any future ones. Horsley takes the "harvest" and vintage here as referring to purifying judgments which cause the excision of the ungodly from the earth, and the placing of the faithful in a state of peace on the earth: not the last judgment (<reference osisRef="John.15.2">Joh 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.15-Rev.14.20">Re 14:15-20</reference>). <div eID="gen14231" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffb4646d77ad7dd410387800e20e8915cb5891b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8643"/><div sID="gen14232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8643"/><hi type="bold">6. birds ... beasts--</hi>transition from the image "sprigs," "branches," to the thing meant: the Assyrian soldiers and leaders shall be the prey of birds and beasts, the whole year through, "winter" and "summer," so numerous shall be their carcasses. Horsley translates the Hebrew which is singular: "upon it," not "upon them"; the "it" refers to God's "dwelling-place" (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Is 18:4</reference>) in the Holy Land, which Antichrist ("the bird of prey" with the "beasts," his rebel hosts) is to possess himself of, and where he is to perish. <div eID="gen14232" type="x-p"/>
entries.b49845d22ef8ea129b95156d0f392221631d8c47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8644"/><div sID="gen14233" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8644"/><hi type="bold">7. present ... people scattered and peeled--</hi>For the right rendering, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Is 18:2</reference>. The repetition of epithets enhances the honor paid to Jehovah by so mighty a nation. The Ethiopians, wonder-struck at such an interposition of Jehovah in behalf of His people, shall send gifts to Jerusalem in His honor (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Is 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.31">Psa 68:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">72:10</reference>). Thus translate: "a present ... from a people." Or translate, as English Version; "the present" will mean "the people" of Ethiopia converted to God (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Ro 15:16</reference>). Horsley takes the people converted to Jehovah, as the Jews in the latter days.<div eID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">place of the name--</hi>where Jehovah peculiarly manifests His glory; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.10">Ac 2:10</reference> and 8:27 show how worshippers came up to Jerusalem from Egypt" and "Ethiopia." Frumentius, an Egyptian, in the fourth century, converted Abyssinia to Christianity; and a Christian church, under an abuna or bishop, still flourishes there. The full accomplishment is probably still future. <chapter eID="Isa.18"/>

entries.9987421bca44bdff7b9c198bccc0b126ccbe419f: <div eID="gen27240" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27241" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27242" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27242" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27241" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27243" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains a very obscure prophecy; possibly designed to give the Jews, and perhaps the Egyptians, whose country is supposed to be meant, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Isa 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference>, and with whom many Jews resided, an indignation of God's interposition in favor of Sion, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.3">Isa 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Isa 18:4</reference>; and of his counsels in regard to the destruction of their common enemy, Sennacherib, whose vast army, just as he thought his projects ripe, and ready to be crowned with success, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.5">Isa 18:5</reference>, should become a prey to the beasts of the field, and to the fowls of heaven, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.6">Isa 18:6</reference>; and that Egypt should be grateful to God for the deliverance vouchsafed her, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference>. <div eID="gen27243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27244" type="x-p"/> This is one of the most obscure prophecies in the whole Book of Isaiah. The subject of it, the end and design of it, the people to whom it is addressed, the history to which it belongs, the person who sends the messengers, and the nation to whom the messengers are sent, are all obscure and doubtful. - L. <div eID="gen27244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27245" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27246" type="x-p"/> Wo to the land - הוי ארץ hoi arets! This interjection should be translated ho! for it is properly a particle of calling: Ho, land! Attend! Give ear! <div eID="gen27246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27247" type="x-p"/> Shadowing with wings "The winged cymbal" - צלצל כנפים tsiltsal kenaphayim. I adopt this as the most probable of the many interpretations that have been given of these words. It is Bochart's: see Phaleg, 4:2. The Egyptian sistrum is expressed by a periphrasis; the Hebrews had no name for it in their language, not having in use the instrument itself. The cymbal they had was an instrument in its use and sound not much unlike the sistrum; and to distinguish it from the sistrum, they called it the cymbal with wings. The cymbal was a round hollow piece of metal, which, being struck against another, gave a ringing sound: the sistrum was a round instrument, consisting of a broad rim of metal, through which from side to side ran several loose laminae or small rods of metal, which being shaken, gave a like sound. These, projecting on each side, had somewhat the appearance of wings; or might be very properly expressed by the same word which the Hebrews used for wings, or for the extremity, or a part of any thing projecting. The sistrum is given in a medal of Adrian, as the proper attribute of Egypt. See Addison on Medals, Series 3. No. 4; where the figure of it may be seen. The frame of the sistrum was in shape rather like the ancient lyre; it was not round. <div eID="gen27247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27248" type="x-p"/> If we translate shadowing with wings, it may allude to the multitude of its vessels, whose sails may be represented under the notion of wings. The second verse seems to support this interpretation. Vessels of bulrushes, גמא gome, or rather the flag papyrus, so much celebrated as the substance on which people wrote in ancient times, and from which our paper is denominated. The sails might have been made of this flag: but whole canoes were constructed from it. Mat sails are used to the present day in China. The Vulgate fully understood the meaning of the word, and has accordingly translated, in vasis papyri, "in vessels of papyrus." Reshi vesselis. - Old MS. Bib. This interpretation does not please Bp. Lowth, and for his dissent he gives the following reasons: - <div eID="gen27248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27249" type="x-p"/> In opposition to other interpretations of these words which have prevailed, it may be briefly observed that צלצל tsiltsel is never used to signify shadow, nor is כנף canaph applied to the sails of ships. If, therefore, the words are rightly interpreted the winged cymbal, meaning the sistrum, Egypt must be the country to which the prophecy is addressed. And upon this hypothesis the version and explanation must proceed. I farther suppose, that the prophecy was delivered before Sennacherib's return from his Egyptian expedition, which took up three years; and that it was designed to give to the Jews, and perhaps likewise to the Egyptians, an intimation of God's counsels in regard to the destruction of their great and powerful enemy. <div eID="gen27249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27250" type="x-p"/> Which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia "Which borders on the rivers of Cush" - What are the rivers of Cush? whether the eastern branches of the lower Nile, the boundary of Egypt towards Arabia, or the parts of the upper Nile towards Ethiopia, it is not easy to determine. The word מעבר meeber signifies either on this side or on the farther side: I have made use of the same kind of ambiguous expression in the translation.
entries.1723de3e2259abfff4123b248e28ae314e7aa3a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27251" type="x-p"/> In vessels of bulrushes "In vessels of papyrus" - This circumstance agrees perfectly well with Egypt. It is well known that the Egyptians commonly used on the Nile a light sort of ships, or boats, made of the reed papyrus. Ex ipso quidem papyro navigia texunt. Pliny, 42:11. <div eID="gen27251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> Conseritur bibula Memphitis cymba papyro. <div eID="gen27252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> Lucan, 4:136. <div eID="gen27253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> Go, ye swift messengers - To this nation before mentioned, who, by the Nile, and by their numerous canals, have the means of spreading the report in the most expeditious manner through the whole country: go, ye swift messengers, and carry this notice of God's designs in regard to them. By the swift messengers are meant, not any particular persons specially appointed to this office, but any of the usual conveyers of news whatsoever, travelers, merchants, and the like, the instruments and agents of common fame. These are ordered to publish this declaration made by the prophet throughout Egypt, and to all the world; and to excite their attention to the promised visible interposition of God. <div eID="gen27254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> Scattered "Stretched out in length" - Egypt, that is, the fruitful part, exclusive of the deserts on each side, is one long vale, through the middle of which runs the Nile, bounded on each side to the east and west by a chain of mountains seven hundred and fifty miles in length; in breadth from one to two or three days' journey: even at the widest part of the Delta, from Pelusium to Alexandria, not above two hundred and fifty miles broad. Egmont and Hayman, and Pococke. <div eID="gen27255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27256" type="x-p"/> Peeled "Smoothed" - Either relating to the practice of the Egyptian priests, who made their bodies smooth by shaving off their hair, (see Herod. 2:37); or rather to their country's being made smooth, perfectly plain and level, by the overflowing of the Nile. <div eID="gen27256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> Meted out "Meted out by line" - It is generally referred to the frequent necessity of having recourse to mensuration in Egypt, in order to determine the boundaries after the inundations of the Nile; to which even the origin of the science of geometry is by some ascribed. Strabo, lib. 17 sub init. <div eID="gen27257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27258" type="x-p"/> Trodden down - Supposed to allude to a peculiar method of tillage in use among the Egyptians. Both Herodotus, (lib. ii.), and Diodorus, (lib. i.), say that when the Nile had retired within its banks, and the ground became somewhat dry, they sowed their land, and then sent in their cattle, (their hogs, says the former), to tread in the seed; and without any farther care expected the harvest. <div eID="gen27258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> The rivers have spoiled "The rivers have nourished" - The word בזאו bazeu is generally taken to be an irregular form for בזזו bazezu, "have spoiled," as four MSS. have it in this place; and so most of the Versions, both ancient and modern, understand it. On which Schultens, Gram. Hebrews p. 491, has the following re; mark:"Ne minimam quidem speciem veri habet בזאו bazau, Esai. <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference>, elatum pro בזזו bazazu, deripiunt. Haec esset anomalia, cui nihil simile in toto linguae ambitu. In talibus nil finire, vel fateri ex mera agi conjectura, tutius justiusque. Radicem בזא baza olim extare potuisse, quis neget? Si cognatum quid sectandum erat, ad בזה bazah, contemsit, potius decurrendum fuisset; ut בזאו bazeu, pro בזו bazu, sit enuntiatum, vel בזיו baziv. Digna phrasis, flumina contemmunt terram, i.e., inundant." "בזא baza, Arab. extulit se superbius, item subjecit sibi: unde praet. pl. בזאו bazeu, subjecerunt sibi, i.e., inundarunt." - Simonis' Lexic. Heb. <div eID="gen27259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> A learned friend has suggested to me another explanation of the word. בזא baza, Syr., and ביזא beiza, Chald., signifies uber, "a dug," mamma, "a breast;" agreeably to which the verb signifies to nourish. This would perfectly well suit with the Nile: whereas nothing can be more discordant than the idea of spoiling and plundering; for to the inundation of the Nile Egypt owed every thing; the fertility of the soil, and the very soil itself. Besides, the overflowing of the Nile came on by gentle degrees, covering with out laying waste the country: "Mira aeque natura fluminis, quod cum caeteri omnes abluant terras et eviscerent, Nilus tanto caeteris major adeo nihil exedit, nec abradit, ut contra adjiciat vires; minimumque in eo sit, quod solum temperet. Illato enim limo arenas saturat ac jungit; debetque illi Aegyptus non tantum fertilitatem terrarum, sed ipsas." - Seneca, Nat. Quaest., 4:2. I take the liberty, therefore, which Schultens seems to think allowable in this place, of hazarding a conjectural interpretation. It is a fact that the Ganges changes its course, and overruns and lays barren whole districts, from which it was a few years back several miles distant. Such changes do not nourish but spoil the ground.
entries.5871a224ac2b91f8efe95018c60f00b62156c195: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> When he lifteth up an ensign "When the standard is lifted up" - I take God to be the Agent in this verse; and that by the standard and the trumpet are meant the meteors, the thunder, the lightning, the storm, earthquake, and tempest, by which Sennacherib's army shall be destroyed, or by which at least the destruction of it shall be accompanied; as it is described in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Isa 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">Isa 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Isa 29:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.31">Isa 30:31</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Psa.76.1-Psa.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference> (note), and the title of it, according to the Septuagint, Vulgate and Aethiopic. They are called, by a bold metaphor, the standard lifted up, and the trumpet sounded. The latter is used by Homer, I think with great force, in his introduction to the battle of the gods; though I find it has disgusted some of the minor critics: - Βραχε δ' ευρεια χθων, Αμφι δε σαλπιγζεν μεγας ουρανος. <div eID="gen27261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> Il. 21:388. "Heaven in loud thunders bids the trumpet sound, <div eID="gen27262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> And wide beneath them groans the rending ground." <div eID="gen27263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27264" type="x-p"/> Pope
entries.ed4824be97741b207f153399c7b5632b39e853f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> For so the Lord said unto me "For thus hath Jehovah said unto me" - The subject of the remaining part of this chapter is, that God would comfort and support his own people, though threatened with immediate destruction by the Assyrians; that Sennacherib's great designs and mighty efforts against them should be frustrated; and that his vast expectations should be rendered abortive, when he thought them mature, and just ready to be crowned with success; that the chief part of his army should be made a prey for the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, (for this is the meaning of the allegory continued through the fifth and sixth verses); and that Egypt, being delivered from his oppression, and avenged by the hand of God of the wrongs which she had suffered, should return thanks for the wonderful deliverance, both of herself and of the Jews, from this most powerful adversary. <div eID="gen27265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> Like a clear heat "Like the clear heat" - The same images are employed by an Arabian poet: - <div eID="gen27266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27267" type="x-p"/> Solis more fervens, dum frigus; quumque ardet <div eID="gen27267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> Sirius, tum vero frigus ipse et umbra. <div eID="gen27268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27269" type="x-p"/> Which is illustrated in the note by a like passage from another Arabian poet: - <div eID="gen27269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27270" type="x-p"/> Calor est hyeme, refrigerium aestate. <div eID="gen27270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> Excerpta ex Hamasa; published by Schultens, at the end of Erpenius's Arabic Grammar, p. 425. <div eID="gen27271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> Upon herbs "After rain" - "אור aur here signifies rain, according to what is said <reference osisRef="Job.36.11">Job 36:11</reference> : 'The cloud scatters his rain.'" - Kimchi. In which place of Job the Chaldee paraphrast does indeed explain אורו auro by מטריה matereyh; and so again <reference osisRef="Job.36.21">Job 36:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.36.30">Job 36:30</reference>. This meaning of the word seems to make the best sense in this place; it is to be wished that it were better supported. <div eID="gen27272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> In the heat of harvest "In the day of harvest" - For בחם bechom, in the heat, fourteen MSS., (several ancient), the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate read ביום beyom, in the day. The mistake seems to have arisen from כחם kechom in the line above.
entries.dbe7ad27dc6e223cdff6af537d714a9fdbad2ca5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> The flower "The blossom" - Hebrews her blossom; נצה nitstsah, that is, the blossom of the vine, גפן gephen, vine, understood, which is of the common gender. See <reference osisRef="Gen.40.10">Gen 40:10</reference>. Note, that by the defective punctuation of this word, many interpreters, and our translators among the rest, have been led into a grievous mistake, (for how can the swelling grape become a blossom?) taking the word נצה nitstsah for the predicate; whereas it is the subject of the proposition, or the nominative case to the verb.
entries.e2a3224829504ddc9e9ee612584e69e0cdcadff3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27275" type="x-p"/> The present "A gift" - The Egyptians were in alliance with the kingdom of Judah, and were fellow-sufferers with the Jews under the invasion of their common enemy Sennacherib; and so were very nearly interested in the great and miraculous deliverance of that kingdom, by the destruction of the Assyrian army. Upon which wonderful event it is said, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.23">2Chr 32:23</reference>, that "many brought gifts unto Jehovah to Jerusalem, and presents to Hezekiah king of Judah; so that he was magnified of all nations from henceforth." It is not to be doubted, that among these the Egyptians distinguished themselves in their acknowledgments on this occasion. <div eID="gen27275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27276" type="x-p"/> Of a people "From a people" - Instead of עם am, a people, the Septuagint and Vulgate read מעם meam, from a people, which is confirmed by the repetition of it in the next line. The difference is of importance; for if this be the true reading, the prediction of the admission of Egypt into the true Church of God is not so explicit as it might otherwise seem to be. However, that event is clearly foretold at the end of the next chapter. - L.  <chapter eID="Isa.18"/> <div eID="gen27276" type="x-p"/>

entries.b4d1587ffee98e32d82bc89c89e704aadc0403f8: <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.3">Isa 18:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13041" type="x-p"/> The prophecy commences with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi>, which never signifies <hi type="italic">heus</hi>, but always <hi type="italic">vae</hi> (woe). Here, however, it differs from <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">Isa 17:12</reference>, and is an expression of compassion (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa 55:1</reference>; Zec 2:10) rather than of anger; for the fact that the mighty Ethiopia is oppressed by the still mightier Asshur, is a humiliation which Jehovah has prepared for the former. <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Isa 18:1</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference></hi>: <hi type="italic">“Woe to the land of the whirring of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush, that sends ambassadors into the sea and in boats of papyrus over the face of the waters.”</hi> The land of Cush commences, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>), where Upper Egypt ends. The <hi type="italic">Sevēneh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Aswân</hi>), mentioned by Ezekiel, is the boundary-point at which the Nile enters <hi type="italic">Mizraim</hi> proper, and which is still a depot for goods coming from the south down the Nile. The <hi type="italic">naharē</hi>-<hi type="italic">Cush</hi> (rivers of Cush) are chiefly those that surround the Cushite <hi type="italic">Seba</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference>). This is the name given to the present Sennâr, the Meroitic island which is enclosed between the White and Blue Nile (the <hi type="italic">Astapos</hi> of Ptolemy, or the present <hi type="italic">Bahr</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Abyad</hi>, and the Astaboras of Ptolemy, or the present <hi type="italic">Bahr</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Azrak</hi>). According to the latest researches, more especially those of Speke, the White Nile, which takes its rise in the Lake of Nyanza, is the chief source of the Nile. The latter, and the Blue Nile, whose confluence (<hi type="italic">makran</hi>) with it takes place in lat. 15° 25´, are fed by many larger or smaller tributary streams (as well as mountain torrents); the Blue Nile even more than the Nile proper. And this abundance of water in the land to the south of <hi type="italic">Sevēnēh</hi>, and still farther south beyond <hi type="italic">Seba</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Meroë</hi>), might very well have been known to the prophet as a general fact. The land “beyond the rivers of Cush” is the land bounded by the sources of the Nile, i.e., (including Ethiopia itself in the stricter sense of the word) the south land under Ethiopian rule that lay still deeper in the heart of the country, the land of its African auxiliary tribes, whose names (which probably include the later Nubians and Abyssinians), as given in <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.3">2Ch 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">Nah 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>, suppose a minuteness of information which has not yet been attained by modern research. To this Ethiopia, which is designated by its farthest limits (compare Zep 3:10, where Wolff, in his book of Judith, erroneously supposes Media to be intended as the Asiatic Cush), the prophets give the strange name of <hi type="italic">eretz</hi> <hi type="italic">tziltzal</hi> <hi type="italic">cenâp</hi>. This has been interpreted as meaning “the land of the wings of an army with clashing arms” by Gesenius and others; but <hi type="italic">cenâphaim</hi> does not occur in this sense, like <hi type="italic">'agappim</hi> in Ezekiel. Others render it “the land of the noise of waves” (Umbreit); but <hi type="italic">cenâphaim</hi> cannot be used of waters except in such a connection as Isa 8:8. Moreover, <hi type="italic">tziltzal</hi> is not a fitting onomatopoetic word either for the clashing of arms or the noise of waves. Others, again, render it “the land of the double shadow” (Grotius, Vitringa, Knobel, and others); but, however appropriate this epithet might be to Ethiopia as a tropical land, it is very hazardous to take the word in a sense which is not sustained by the usage of the language; and the same objection may be brought against Luzzatto’s “land of the far-shadowing defence.” Shelling has also suggested another objection - namely, that the shadow thrown even in tropical lands is not a double one, falling northwards and southwards at the same time, and therefore that it cannot be figuratively described as double-winged. <hi type="italic">Tziltzal</hi> <hi type="italic">cenâphaim</hi> is the buzzing of the wings of insects, with which Egypt and Ethiopia swarmed on account of the climate and the abundance of water: צלצל, <hi type="italic">constr</hi>. צלצל, <hi type="italic">tinnitus</hi>, <hi type="italic">stridor</hi>, a primary meaning from which the other three meanings of the word-cymbal, harpoon (a whirring dart), and grasshopper<note placement="foot">Schröring supposes <hi type="italic">tziltzal</hi> to be the <hi type="italic">scarabaeus sacer</hi> (Linn.); but it would be much more natural, if any particular animal is intended, to think of the <hi type="italic">tzaltzalya</hi>, as it is called in the language of the Gallas, the <hi type="italic">tzetze</hi> in the Betschuana language, the most dreaded diptera of the interior of Africa, a species of <hi type="italic">glossina</hi> which attacks all the larger <hi type="italic">mammalia</hi> (though not men). Vid., Hartmann, <hi type="italic">Naturgeschichtlich-medic</hi>. <hi type="italic">Skizze der Nilländer</hi>, Abth. i. p. 205.</note>  - are derived. In <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference> the forces of Egypt are called “the fly from the end of the rivers of Egypt.” Here Egypt and Ethiopia are called the land of the whirring of wings, inasmuch as the prophet had in his mind, under the designation of swarms of insects, the motley swarms of different people included in this great kingdom that were so fabulously strange to an Asiatic. Within this great kingdom messengers were now passing to and fro upon its great waters in boats of papyrus (on <hi type="italic">gōme</hi>, Copt. <hi type="italic">‛gōme</hi>, Talm. <hi type="italic">gâmi</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Job.8.11">Job 8:11</reference>), Greek βαρίδες παπύριναι (βαρίς, from the Egyptian <hi type="italic">bari</hi>, <hi type="italic">bali</hi>, a barque). In such vessels as these, and with Egyptian tackle, they went as far as the remote island of Taprobane. The boats were made to clap together (<hi type="italic">pilcatiles</hi>), so as to be carried past the cataracts (Parthey on <hi type="italic">Plutarch. de Iside</hi>, pp. 198-9). And it is to these messengers in their paper boats that the appeal of the prophet is addressed. <div eID="gen13041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13042" type="x-p"/> He sends them home; and what they are to say to their own people is generalized into an announcement to the whole earth. <hi type="italic">“Go, swift messengers, to the people stretched out and polished, to the terrible people far away on the other side, to the nation of command upon command and treading down, whose land rivers cut through. All ye possessors of the globe and inhabitants of the earth, when a banner rises on the mountains, look ye; and when they blow the trumpets, hearken!”</hi> We learn from what follows to what it is that the attention of Ethiopia and all the nations of the earth is directed: it is the destruction of Asshur by Jehovah. They are to attend, when they observe the two signals, the banner and the trumpet-blast; these are decisive moments. Because Jehovah was about to deliver the world from the conquering might of Assyria, against which the Ethiopian kingdom was now summoning all the means of self-defence, the prophet sends the messengers home. Their own people, to which he sends them home, are elaborately described. They are <hi type="italic">memusshâk</hi>, stretched out, i.e., very tall (lxx ἔθνος μετέωρον), just as the Sabaeans are said to have been in Isa 45:14. They are also <hi type="italic">mōrât</hi> = <hi type="italic">memorât</hi> (Ges. §52, Anm. 6), smoothed, <hi type="italic">politus</hi>, i.e., either not disfigured by an ugly growth of hair, or else, without any reference to depilation, but rather with reference to the bronze colour of their skin, smooth and shining with healthy freshness. The description which Herodotus gives of the Ethiopians, μέγιστοι καὶ κάλλιστοι ἀνθρώπων πάντων (iii. 20), quite answers to these first two predicates. They are still further described, with reference to the wide extent of their kingdom, which reached to the remotest south, as “the terrible nation והלאה מן־הוּא,” i.e., from this point, where the prophet meets with the messengers, farther and farther off (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.21-1Sam.20.22">1Sa 20:21-22</reference>, but not <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:9</reference>, where the expression has a chronological meaning, which would be less suitable here, where everything is so pictorial, and which is also to be rejected, because מן־הוּא cannot be equivalent to הוּא מאשׁר; cf., <reference osisRef="Nah.2.9">Nah 2:9</reference>). We may see from <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa 28:13</reference>, what <hi type="italic">kâv</hi> (<hi type="italic">kăv</hi>, with connecting accusatives and before <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi>), a measuring or levelling line, signifies, when used by the prophet with the reduplication which he employs here: it is a people of “command upon command,” - that is to say, a commanding nation; (according to Ewald, Knobel, and others, <hi type="italic">kâv</hi> is equivalent to the Arabic <hi type="italic">kūwe</hi>, strength, a nation of double or gigantic strength.) “<hi type="italic">A people of treading down</hi>” (sc., of others; <hi type="italic">mebūsah</hi> is a second genitive to <hi type="italic">goi</hi>), i.e., one which subdues and tramples down wherever it appears. These are all distinctive predicates - a nation of imposing grandeur, a ruling and conquering nation. The last predicate extols its fertile land. בּזא we take not in the sense of diripere, or as equivalent to <hi type="italic">bâzaz</hi>, like מאס, to melt, equivalent to <hi type="italic">mâsas</hi>, but in the sense of <hi type="italic">findere</hi>, i.e., as equivalent to בזע, like גּמא, to sip = גּמע. For it is no praise to say that a land is scoured out, or washed away, by rivers. Böttcher, who is wrong in describing this chapter as “perhaps the most difficult in the whole of the Old Testament,” very aptly compares with it the expression used by Herodotus (ii. 108), κατετμήθη ἡ Αἴγυπτος. But why this strange elaboration instead of the simple name? There is a divine irony in the fact that a nation so great and glorious, and (though not without reason, considering its natural gifts) so full of self-consciousness, should be thrown into such violent agitation in the prospect of the danger that threatened it, and should be making such strenuous exertions to avert that danger, when Jehovah the God of Israel was about to destroy the threatening power itself in a night, and consequently all the care and trouble of Ethiopia were utterly needless.
entries.cde67fbc2747ad937b8e59f380440b9781dd6531: <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4-Isa.18.6">Isa 18:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen13042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13043" type="x-p"/> The prophet knows for certain that the messengers may be home and announce this act of Jehovah to their own people and to all the world. <hi type="italic">“For thus hath Jehovah spoken to me: I will be still, and will observe upon my throne during clear weather in sunshine, during a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. For before the harvest, when the blossom falls off, and the fruit becomes the ripening grape: then will He cut off the branches with pruning-hooks; and the tendrils He removes, breaks off. They are left altogether to the birds of prey on the mountains, and to the cattle of the land; and the birds of prey summer thereon, and all the cattle of the land will winter thereon.”</hi> The prophecy explains itself here, as is very frequently the case, especially with Isaiah; for the literal words of v. 6 show us unquestionably what it is that Jehovah will allow to develop itself so prosperously under favourable circumstances, and without any interposition on His part, until He suddenly and violently puts an end to the whole, must as it is approaching perfect maturity. It is the might of Assyria. Jehovah quietly looks on from the heavenly seat of His glorious presence, without disturbing the course of the thing intended. This quietness, however, is not negligence, but, as the hortative expressions show, a well-considered resolution. The two <hi type="italic">Caphs</hi> in v. 4 are not comparative, but indicate the time. He remains quiet whilst there is clear weather with sunshine (עלי indicating continuance, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18">Jer 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sa 14:32</reference>), and whilst there is a dew-cloud in the midst of that warmth, which is so favourable for the harvest, by causing the plants that have been thoroughly heated in the day and refreshed at night by the dew, to shoot up and ripen with rapidity and luxuriance. The plant thought of, as v. 5 clearly shows, is the vine. By <hi type="italic">liphnē</hi> <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi> (before the harvest) we are either to understand the period just before the wheat-harvest, which coincides with the flowering of the grape; or, since Isaiah uses <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi> for <hi type="italic">bâzri</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>, the time at the close of the summer, immediately preceding the vintage. Here again the <hi type="italic">Caph</hi> indicates the time. When the blossoming is over, so that the flower fades away, and the fruit that has set becomes a ripening grape (<hi type="italic">boser</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.33">Job 15:33</reference>, not in the sense of <hi type="italic">labruscum</hi>, but of <hi type="italic">omphax</hi>; and <hi type="italic">gâmal</hi>, <hi type="italic">maturescere</hi>, as in Num 17:8, <hi type="italic">maturare</hi>), He cuts off the branches (<hi type="italic">zalzalilm</hi>, from <hi type="italic">zilzēl</hi>, to swing to and fro; compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">dâliye</hi>, a vine-branch, from <hi type="italic">dalâ</hi>, to hang long and loose) upon which the nearly ripened grapes are hanging, and removes or nips off<note placement="foot">התז = התז with a pausal sharpening of the <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>, which is lengthened by the tone, from <hi type="italic">tâzaz</hi> or <hi type="italic">tı̄z</hi> in post-biblical Hebrew, to knock off, knock to pieces, or weaken (compare <hi type="italic">tâshash</hi>). On this change of vowels in pause, see at <reference osisRef="Gen.17.14">Gen 17:14</reference>; and compare Olshausen, §91, d. For an example of the post-biblical use of the word, vid., <hi type="italic">b. Sanhedrin</hi> 102 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, “like two sticks <hi type="italic">hammattı̄zōth</hi>,” i.e., one of which “hits the other in two” (<hi type="italic">hittiz</hi>, apparently from <hi type="italic">tūz</hi>, or <hi type="italic">tiz</hi>, like <hi type="italic">hinnı̄ach</hi> from <hi type="italic">nuach</hi>).</note> the tendrils (<hi type="italic">netishoth</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.5.10">Jer 5:10</reference>, from <hi type="italic">nâtash</hi>, to stretch far out; <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, to twist about a long way, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>); an intentional asyndeton with a pictorial sound. The words of Jehovah concerning Himself have here passed imperceptibly into words of the prophet concerning Jehovah. The ripening grapes, as <reference osisRef="Isa.18.6">Isa 18:6</reference> now explains, are the Assyrians, who were not far from the summit of their power; the fruit-branches that are cut off and nipped in pieces are their corpses, which are now through both summer and winter the food of swarms of summer birds, as well as of beasts of prey that remain the whole winter through. This is the act of divine judgment, to which the approaching exaltation of the banner, and the approaching blast of trumpets, is to call the attention of the people of Ethiopia.
entries.90e5dd736a6fc28d719b1e8fa9e0036e46d65544: <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference> <div eID="gen13043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> What effect this act of Jehovah would have upon the Ethiopian kingdom, if it should now take place, is described in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference> : <hi type="italic">“At that time will there be offered as a homage to Jehovah of hosts a nation stretched out and polished, and from a terrible people, far away on the other side; a nation of command upon command and treading down, whose land rivers cut through, at the place of the name of Jehovah of hosts, the mountain of Zion.”</hi> עם (a people), at the commencement, cannot possibly be equivalent to מעם (from a people). If it were taken in this sense, it would be necessary to make the correction accordingly, as Knobel has done; but the important parallels in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.20">Isa 66:20</reference> and Zep 3:10 are against this. Consequently <hi type="italic">‛am</hi> and <hi type="italic">goi</hi> (people and nation) must be rendered as subjects; and the מן in מעם must be taken as partitive. Ethiopia is offered, i.e., offers itself, as a free-will offering to Jehovah, impelled irresistibly by the force of the impression made by the mighty act of Jehovah, or, as it is expressed in “the Titan among the Psalms” (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.32">Psa 68:32</reference>, probably a Davidic psalm of the time of Hezekiah), “there come kingdoms of splendour out of Egypt; Cush rapidly stretches out its hands to <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>.” In order that the greatness of this spiritual conquest might be fully appreciated, the description of this strangely glorious people is repeated here; and with this poetical rounding, the prophecy itself, which was placed as a kind of overture before the following <hi type="italic">massa Mitzraim</hi> when the prophet collected the whole of his prophecies together, is brought to a close. The Oracle Concerning Egypt  - Isaiah 19 <div eID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13045" type="x-p"/> The three prophecies in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.7.19">Isa 18:1-7, 19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference> really form a trilogy. The first (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference>), which, like chapter 1, the introduction to the whole, is without any special heading, treats in language of the sublimest pathos of <hi type="italic">Ethiopia</hi>. The second (chapter 19) treats in a calmer and more descriptive tone of <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi>. The third (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference>) treats of both <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ethiopia</hi> in the style of historic prose. The kingdom to which all three prophecies refer is one and the same, viz., the Egypto-Ethiopian kingdom; but whilst <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference> refers to the ruling nation, chapter 19 treats of the conquered one, and <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference> embraces both together. The reason why such particular attention is given to Egypt in the prophecy, is that no nation on earth was so mixed up with the history of the kingdom of God, from the patriarchal times downwards, as Egypt was. And because Israel, as the law plainly enjoined upon it, was never to forget that it had been sheltered for a long time in Egypt, and there had grown into a great nation, and had received many benefits; whenever prophecy has to speak concerning Egypt, it is quite as earnest in its promises as it is in its threats. And thus the <hi type="italic">massa</hi> of Isaiah falls into two distinct halves, viz., a threatening one (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.15">Isa 19:1-15</reference>), and a promising one (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.18-Isa.19.25">Isa 19:18-25</reference>); whilst between the judgment and the salvation (in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Isa 19:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">Isa 19:17</reference>) there stands the alarm, forming as it were a connecting bridge between the two. And just in proportion as the coil of punishments is unfolded on the one hand by the prophet, the promise is also unfolded in just as many stages on the other; and moving on in ever new grooves, rises at length to such a height, that it breaks not only through the limits of contemporaneous history, but even through those of the Old Testament itself, and speaks in the spiritual language of the world-embracing love of the New Testament.  <chapter eID="Isa.18"/> <div eID="gen13045" type="x-p"/>

1. Woe to the land. I cannot determine with certainty what is the nation of which Isaiah speaks, though he shews plainly that it bordered on Ethiopia. Some consider it to refer to the whole of Egypt; but this is a mistake, for in the next chapter he treats of Egypt separately, from which it is evident that the people here meant were distinct from the Egyptians. Some think that the Troglodytes are here meant, which does not appear to me to be probable, for they had no intercourse with other nations, because their language, as geographers tell us, was hissing and not speech;
“The Ethiopian Troglodytes,” says Herodotus “are the swiftest of foot of all men of whom we have received any accounts. The Troglodytes feed on serpents, and lizards, and reptiles of that sort, and the language which they have adopted has no resemblance to any other, but they screech like bats. — Herod. 4:183.

FT271 “Scattered and peeled, or, outspread and polished.” — Eng. Ver.
FT272 “A nation meted out and trodden down.” Heb. “A nation of line, and line, and treading under foot.” — Eng. Ver.
FT273 “A nation meted out by line, that is, utterly subdued. Heb. Put under line and line, to decide what part of them should be destroyed, and what saved by the conquerors. In this manner David is described, (2 Samuel 8:2,) as having dealt with the children of Moab. See Lamentations 2:8. Such a nation might well deserve to be called drawn out and pilled, that is drawn through the fingers (or an instrument) like a willow, in order to be peeled and made fit for wicker work.” — Stock.

FT275 “See ye.” “Hear ye.” — Eng. Ver.
FT276 “And I will consider in my dwelling-place.” — Eng. Ver. “I will rest, and look round in my dwelling-place.” — Stock.

FT278 Like the clear heat at the coming of daylight. The resting of Jehovah, hovering over the enemy till they are ripe for destruction, is here beautifully compared to the condensed gloom before daylight, which is wont to usher in a hot summer’s day, and to the sheet of dew that appears to hang over the ground in harvest time presently after sunset. עלי, (ălē,) is here used for near the time of, as we say, against such a time. עלי אור, (ălēōr,) prope lucem, adventante luce. — Stock.
